meta.title: Filter bubbles and explainable recommendation: paraphrase notes
meta.note: Every passage is a paraphrase note written for this project, not a verbatim quotation. Do not cite these passages as if they were the authors exact words.
meta.aliases_note: Registered names for each source. A question that names one of them gets that source's notes boosted; see litlens/retrieval.py.

passages.source: Pariser, E. (2011). The Filter Bubble: What the Internet Is Hiding from You. Penguin Press.
passages.en: Personalised filters decide what we see before we see it. Because the ranking is invisible, users cannot tell that their view of the world has been narrowed; Pariser calls this the filter bubble.

passages.source: Pariser, E. (2011). The Filter Bubble: What the Internet Is Hiding from You. Penguin Press.
passages.en: Pariser argues that escaping the bubble needs two things from the platform: visibility of the filtering rules, and controls that let the user adjust the balance between comfortable and challenging content.

passages.source: Tintarev, N., & Masthoff, J. (2015). Explaining recommendations: Design and evaluation. In Recommender Systems Handbook (pp. 353-382). Springer.
passages.en: Tintarev and Masthoff group the goals of a recommendation explanation into transparency, scrutability, trust, effectiveness, persuasiveness, efficiency and satisfaction. A single explanation rarely serves all seven at once.

passages.source: Tintarev, N., & Masthoff, J. (2015). Explaining recommendations: Design and evaluation. In Recommender Systems Handbook (pp. 353-382). Springer.
passages.en: Most explanation work is one-directional: the system explains why an item was recommended, and the user reads it. Explanations inform the user but usually do not let the user change the algorithm's behaviour.

passages.source: Bostandjiev, S., O'Donovan, J., & Hollerer, T. (2012). TasteWeights: A visual interactive hybrid recommender system. RecSys '12, 35-42.
passages.en: TasteWeights is an interactive hybrid recommender. Users see the weights of features and social connections, drag them, and the recommendation list updates immediately, so the model's reasoning becomes something they can manipulate.

passages.source: Bostandjiev, S., O'Donovan, J., & Hollerer, T. (2012). TasteWeights: A visual interactive hybrid recommender system. RecSys '12, 35-42.
passages.en: In TasteWeights the user stays the final decision maker: the system suggests, the user inspects and edits the weights, and control can be handed back at any point.

passages.source: He, C., Parra, D., & Verbert, K. (2016). Interactive recommender systems: A survey. Expert Systems with Applications, 56, 9-27.
passages.en: He, Parra and Verbert survey interactive recommender systems and classify them by how the user takes part: visualisation of the item space, critiquing of recommendations, and direct editing of preference models.

passages.source: He, C., Parra, D., & Verbert, K. (2016). Interactive recommender systems: A survey. Expert Systems with Applications, 56, 9-27.
passages.en: The same survey warns that exposing many parameters at once causes cognitive overload, and that interactive recommenders are hard to evaluate because the user's behaviour changes the system under test.

passages.source: Ekstrand, M. D., Harper, F. M., Willemsen, M. C., & Konstan, J. A. (2014). User perception of differences in recommender algorithms. RecSys '14, 161-168.
passages.en: Ekstrand and colleagues found that users are poor at telling recommender algorithms apart. Differences between algorithms are often invisible in the interface, so users form impressions from interface cues rather than from the algorithm.

passages.source: Lee, J. D., & See, K. A. (2004). Trust in automation: Designing for appropriate reliance. Human Factors, 46(1), 50-80.
passages.en: Lee and See describe trust as an attitude that should be calibrated: over-trust leads to over-reliance and missed errors, under-trust leads to disuse. Good design supports appropriate reliance rather than maximum trust.

passages.source: Amershi, S., et al. (2019). Guidelines for human-AI interaction. CHI '19, 1-13.
passages.en: Amershi and colleagues set out 18 guidelines for human-AI interaction, grouped by when they apply: initially, during interaction, when the system is wrong, and over time. One guideline is to scope the service when in doubt.

passages.source: Amershi, S., et al. (2019). Guidelines for human-AI interaction. CHI '19, 1-13.
passages.en: Other guidelines ask the system to make clear what it can do, support efficient correction, explain why it did what it did, and notify users when its behaviour changes. Together they treat error recovery as part of the interaction, not an afterthought.

passages.source: Norman, D. A. (1988). The Design of Everyday Things. Basic Books.
passages.en: Norman's seven-stage model separates the gulf of execution (can I work out what to do?) from the gulf of evaluation (can I tell what happened?). Interfaces should narrow both, not just the first.

passages.source: Shneiderman, B. (1983). Direct manipulation: A step beyond programming languages. IEEE Transactions on Computers, 32(8), 57-69.
passages.en: Direct manipulation, as Shneiderman defined it, has three properties: continuous representation of the objects, physical actions instead of typed commands, and rapid, incremental, reversible operations whose effect is immediately visible.

passages.source: Nielsen, J. (1994). Heuristic evaluation. In Usability Inspection Methods. Wiley.
passages.en: Nielsen's heuristics include visibility of system status, user control and freedom, error prevention, and helping users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors. Each assumes the user can see the state of the system while acting.

passages.source: Horvitz, E. (1999). Principles of mixed-initiative user interfaces. CHI '99, 159-166.
passages.en: Horvitz's mixed-initiative principles ask designers to weigh the user's uncertainty, the cost of a wrong action and the cost of interrupting, and to let initiative pass between human and system rather than fixing it once.

passages.source: Lewis, P., et al. (2020). Retrieval-augmented generation for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks. NeurIPS '20.
passages.en: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds an answer in passages retrieved for the question. It reduces fabrication, but the quality of the answer is bounded by retrieval: if the right passage is not retrieved, the model has nothing reliable to cite.
